Section 01The two questions that the spectrum must answer

The PNAS paper asks whether collective light–matter coupling can protect coherence between the upper and lower polaritons, and whether nonlinear spectra can independently reveal the accompanying reduction in vibrational dressing. These questions lead to two different observables: the waiting-time oscillation of a cross-peak and the nodal line between positive and negative contributions near the lower-polariton diagonal peak.

The mechanism is not simply that a photon has no molecular vibration. Delocalization reduces a polariton's diagonal coupling to independent local environments, but the same environments also connect polaritons to a large manifold of dark states. Cavity leakage adds another channel. A useful explanation must therefore keep the bright and dark sectors, distinguish diagonal noise from population transfer, and retain the doubly excited manifold needed for excited-state absorption.

We begin with explicit finite matrices, build the third-order response from successive optical interactions, and then connect the spectrum to coherence and spectral diffusion. The paper's production method is Lindblad–partially linearized density matrix dynamics, abbreviated L-PLDM. The teaching code supplied here instead uses exact finite-system Lindblad propagation for small models; it tests algebra and response conventions, not the paper's full non-Markovian simulations.

Reading route. Sections 2–10 construct the model and its environmental couplings. Sections 11–21 derive excitation manifolds, dipole matrices, response pathways, Fourier conventions, and cavity loss. Sections 22–29 connect the simulations to rates, time scales, nodal lines, and numerical algorithms. The final sections contain a calculator, validation checks, and worked exercises.

Source: PNAS, abstract and introduction. The paper reports theoretical predictions for a CdSe-nanoplatelet-inspired model, not a new experimental observation of the proposed long-lived beating.

Section 02The Hilbert space and the local electronic basis

Molecule or emitter n has an electronic ground ket |gn⟩ and excited ket |en⟩. The cavity contains a harmonic photon mode. Each emitter also has an independent harmonic environment. The total space is

H=[⨂n=1NCn2]⊗Fc⊗[⨂nνFnν].
(1)

Define σ^n=|gn⟩⟨en|, n^n=|en⟩⟨en|, the photon annihilator a^, and bath annihilators b^nν. In the local electronic basis (|gn⟩,|en⟩),

[σ^n]=(0100),[n^n]=(0001),σ^n2=0.
(2)

The bath oscillators and cavity are not two-level systems. In particular, a^|2⟩=2|1⟩, and this factor becomes essential in the two-excitation manifold. Local electronic operators on distinct emitters commute because they act in different tensor-product factors.

To keep dimensions explicit, use gE=ℏgc for the energy-valued coupling per emitter, Ec=ℏωc for the cavity energy, and ϵ for the bare electronic transition energy. We use G=NgE for the collective coupling energy; the full resonant splitting is 2G.

Section 03The Holstein–Tavis–Cummings Hamiltonian

With identical emitters and real uniform coupling, the model can be written

H^=H^s⊗I^b+I^s⊗H^b+∑nn^n⊗B^n,
(3)
H^s=ϵ∑nn^n+Eca^†a^+gE∑n(σ^n†a^+a^†σ^n),H^b=∑nνℏωνb^nν†b^nν,B^n=∑νdν(b^nν†+b^nν).
(4)

Here dν has units of energy. The coupling is diagonal in the local electronic basis: an electronic excitation changes the equilibrium position of that site's bath. The environments need not be memoryless. The paper uses a slowly relaxing Drude–Lorentz bath to represent their correlation spectrum.

An equivalent mass-weighted coordinate convention is B^n=∑νcνQ^nν, with Q^ν=ℏ/(2ων)(b^ν+b^ν†). Thus dν=cνℏ/(2ων). The apparent prefactors in spectral densities differ between these conventions; one should transform the coefficients instead of mixing formulas from both.

Completing the square for an excited site gives a relaxation energy λ=∑νdν2/(ℏων). Whether ϵ denotes a vertical or relaxed transition energy depends on whether this shift has already been included as a counterterm. The Hamiltonian above has no extra counterterm, so its relaxed minimum is lower by λ.

Source: main Eq. (1) and Eqs. (21)–(22). The energy-valued coupling convention here makes the unit conversions explicit.

Section 04The one-excitation Hamiltonian as a matrix

Let |0⟩=|g1⋯gN;0c⟩. Define |c⟩=a^†|0⟩ and |n⟩=σ^n†|0⟩. In the ordered basis B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,…,|N⟩),

[H^s]B1=(EcgEgE⋯gEgEϵ0⋯0gE0ϵ⋯0⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮gE00⋯ϵ),[n^n]B1=|n⟩⟨n| in this representation.
(5)

A bath configuration adds a site-dependent diagonal shift to the corresponding molecular entry, not to the cavity entry. Even when the average molecular energies are identical, a given fluctuating bath configuration is not generally permutation symmetric.

For N=2, define |B⟩=(|1⟩+|2⟩)/2 and |D⟩=(|1⟩−|2⟩)/2. In (|c⟩,|B⟩,|D⟩), the Hamiltonian is

[H^s]=(Ec2gE02gEϵ000ϵ).
(6)

This basis makes the optically coupled two-by-two block visible. It does not remove the dark state from the bath-coupled dynamics.

Section 05Bright, dark, upper, and lower polariton kets

For general N, define |B⟩=N−1/2∑n|n⟩, with any orthonormal set of N−1 dark kets orthogonal to it. One choice is the discrete Fourier basis

|Dk⟩=1N∑n=1Ne2πikn/N|n⟩,k=1,…,N−1.
(7)

The conjugate phase belongs in the bra. Orthogonality follows from the geometric-series sum of roots of unity. The coupled block in (|c⟩,|B⟩) is (EcGGϵ). Set δE=Ec−ϵ, D=δE2+4G2, and θ=12atan2(2G,δE) for G>0. Then

EU=Ec+ϵ+D2,EL=Ec+ϵ−D2,
(8)
|U⟩=cos⁡θ|c⟩+sin⁡θ|B⟩,|L⟩=−sin⁡θ|c⟩+cos⁡θ|B⟩.
(9)

The matter fractions and photon fractions are

xU=sin2⁡θ=12(1−δED),xL=cos2⁡θ=12(1+δED),cU=1−xU,cL=1−xL.
(10)

At resonance, all four fractions are one half and EU−EL=2G. For a cavity far above the molecular transition, the upper branch becomes photon-like, while the lower branch becomes matter-like. This limit checks the signs in the mixing-angle convention. Another overall phase for |L⟩ is physically equivalent, but its bath matrix elements and coherences must then be transformed consistently.

Source: Eqs. (2)–(5). The basis and phase convention here are fixed explicitly to avoid detuning-sign ambiguity.

Section 06Transform the local baths, rather than replacing them by one bath

Let Cnα=⟨n|α⟩ be the molecular component of polariton or dark ket |α⟩. In the dressed basis, the system–bath coupling is

H^sb=∑αβ|α⟩⟨β|⊗B^αβ,B^αβ=∑nCnα∗CnβB^n.
(11)

The diagonal operators fluctuate the dressed-state energies. The off-diagonal operators induce transitions and mix coherences. Dropping the latter is an additional approximation, not a consequence of the basis transformation.

For two molecules on resonance, use the ordered basis (|U⟩,|L⟩,|D⟩), with the phase choice from Section 5. Put B^Σ=B^1+B^2, B^Δ=B^1−B^2. Direct multiplication gives

[H^sb]=(B^Σ/4B^Σ/4B^Δ/(22)B^Σ/4B^Σ/4B^Δ/(22)B^Δ/(22)B^Δ/(22)B^Σ/2).
(12)

Every entry is an operator on the bath space. The matrix describes a system operator whose coefficients are bath operators; it is not a three-by-three numerical Hamiltonian until a bath representation is supplied. The antisymmetric bath fluctuation connects both polaritons to the dark state. Averaging the two environments before transforming would erase precisely this channel.

Section 07Derive the reduction in diagonal reorganization energy

For independent identical local environments, the equilibrium correlation is ⟨B^n(t)B^m(0)⟩=δnmC(t). The diagonal dressed-state correlation therefore is

Cα(t)=⟨B^αα(t)B^αα(0)⟩=∑n|Cnα|4C(t).
(13)

Since the reorganization energy is linear in the spectral density, the same weights give

λα=λ∑n|Cnα|4.
(14)

For a uniformly delocalized matter component with matter fraction xα, each |Cnα|2=xα/N. Thus

λα=λxα2N,λU=λL=λ4Nat resonance.
(15)

There are two reductions: mixing with the photon gives xα2, while spreading the matter amplitude over independent sites gives 1/N. The bath-force amplitude and its variance should not be confused; squaring the amplitude is what produces the reorganization-energy factor.

For correlated environments, the general expression contains a double sum, ∑nm|Cnα|2|Cmα|2Cnm(t). A perfectly common bath instead yields xα2C(t), without the 1/N suppression. The independence assumption is therefore part of the mechanism.

For a nonuniform matter distribution, define normalized molecular weights wnα=|Cnα|2/xα. Then λα=λxα2∑nwnα2, involving an inverse participation ratio rather than the literal molecule count.

Section 08Relative coherence noise is not the noise of one polariton

A coherence |U⟩⟨L| accumulates the difference between two energies. In a diagonal-noise approximation, its fluctuation operator is Δ^B=B^UU−B^LL. For independent baths,

CULdiff(t)=∑n(|CnU|2−|CnL|2)2C(t)=(xU−xL)2NC(t).
(16)

At exact resonance, xU=xL=1/2, so the relative diagonal noise cancels in this ideal homogeneous model. Nevertheless, the off-diagonal bath matrix elements from Section 6 remain nonzero. They produce population relaxation, polariton mixing, and dark-state scattering, and cavity leakage also remains.

Consequently, λ/(4N) is a useful diagonal-dressing scale, but it is not by itself a complete formula for the decay time of ρUL. A model that predicts infinite coherence solely from this cancellation has omitted the other channels. This distinction is especially important when interpreting a nonlinear spectrum, whose amplitude contains both waiting-time coherences and optical-coherence evolution in the first and third intervals.

Section 09The dark manifold: weak individual channels, many destinations

For a resonant uniform polariton and one normalized dark ket, the squared system matrix elements of the local projectors sum to 1/(2N). Summing over the N−1 dark destinations gives

∑d=1N−1∑n=1N|⟨Dd|n^n|U⟩|2=N−12N.
(17)

One derivation uses dark-space completeness, ∑d|Dd⟩⟨Dd|=I^mol−|B⟩⟨B|. For each site, the diagonal element of this projector is 1−1/N; multiplying by |⟨n|U⟩|2=1/(2N) and summing yields the result.

This sum approaches one half, not zero, as N→∞. Delocalization weakens a particular channel, but the number of channels grows. Protection against dark-state transfer therefore also depends on the bath's spectral weight at the energy gap. At resonance, the upper-to-dark gap is G, half the upper–lower splitting.

The paper combines this spectral bottleneck with reduced diagonal dressing and finite cavity lifetime. These are complementary mechanisms, not interchangeable explanations of the same single parameter.

Section 10Bath correlations and an explicit unit convention

For one harmonic mode, b^(t)=e−iωtb^, ⟨b^†b^⟩=nB, and ⟨b^b^†⟩=nB+1. Therefore

C(t)=∑νdν2[(nB(ων)+1)e−iωνt+nB(ων)eiωνt].
(18)

Define an energy-domain spectral density j(E)=π∑νdν2δ(E−ℏων). With this convention,

C(t)=1π∫0∞j(E)[coth⁡βE2cos⁡Etℏ−isin⁡Etℏ]dE,λ=1π∫0∞j(E)EdE.
(19)

The Drude–Lorentz form and its high-temperature leading correlation are

j(E)=2λγEEE2+γE2,C(t)≃(2λkBT−iλγE)e−γEt/ℏ,τb=ℏγE.
(20)

The first expression has the prescribed reorganization energy because ∫0∞γE/(E2+γE2)dE=π/2. The second is a high-temperature approximation, not the exact quantum correlation at arbitrary temperature. Its omitted thermal exponential terms can matter when the bath frequencies are not small compared with kBT.

The paper uses λ=50cm−1≃6.20meV and γE=18cm−1≃2.23meV. With ℏ=658.2119569meVfs, the memory scale is about 295fs. It is not generally safe to replace that environment by a memoryless dephasing rate over all relevant waiting times.

Source: model parameters and Eqs. (21)–(22). The frequency-to-energy spectral-density conversion is defined here before using any golden-rule formula.

Section 11Why a two-dimensional spectrum needs two excitations

A third-order signal contains an excited-state absorption pathway: after the first two interactions prepare an excited population or coherence, the third interaction can raise it into the two-excitation manifold. A model restricted to |0⟩ and the first manifold cannot represent this contribution.

The basis counts through two total excitations are

d0=1,d1=N+1,d2=1+N+(N2),d≤2=N2+3N+62.
(21)

The two-excitation kets are |2c⟩=(a^†)2|0⟩/2, |c,n⟩=a^†σ^n†|0⟩, and |n,m⟩=σ^n†σ^m†|0⟩ with n<m. There is no |n,n⟩, because an emitter is two-level.

For two emitters, in B2=(|2c⟩,|c,1⟩,|c,2⟩,|1,2⟩),

[H^s]B2=(2Ec2gE2gE02gEEc+ϵ0gE2gE0Ec+ϵgE0gEgE2ϵ).
(22)

Each 2 follows from annihilating one photon in |2c⟩. Each coupling to |1,2⟩ is only gE, because the photon occupation there changes from one to zero. The bath operator n^1 is diagonal with entries (0,1,0,1) in this basis; n^2 has entries (0,0,1,1). Thus a doubly excited molecular ket couples to both local environments.

Section 12The symmetric two-excitation block and its anharmonicity

For general N≥2, define |cB⟩=N−1/2∑n|c,n⟩ and the symmetric two-molecule excitation |B2⟩=(N2)−1/2∑n<m|n,m⟩. The symmetric two-excitation matrix is

[H^s](|2c⟩,|cB⟩,|B2⟩)=(2EcgE2N0gE2NEc+ϵgE2(N−1)0gE2(N−1)2ϵ).
(23)

On resonance its eigenvalues are 2ϵ and 2ϵ±gE4N−2. Two independent harmonic polaritons would instead give outer energies 2ϵ±2gEN. The difference comes from saturation: after one molecule is excited, only N−1 remain available for another molecular excitation.

This slight mismatch matters spectroscopically. Ground-state bleach and stimulated emission probe ground-to-first-manifold transitions, whereas excited-state absorption probes first-to-second-manifold transitions. If the relevant transitions and dipole factors formed a perfectly harmonic ladder, the third-order response to a linear dipole would cancel. Hard-core saturation prevents that exact cancellation.

For N=2, the outer two-excitation shifts are ±6gE, not ±22gE. The companion code checks this spectrum directly. It also retains nonsymmetric states in the full small-system basis, since local baths or loss can connect sectors that an isolated symmetric Hamiltonian leaves separate.

Section 13Constructing the dipole matrices

For aligned transition dipoles and detection through the matter polarization, use

μ^=μ^++μ^−,μ^+=μ0∑nσ^n†,μ^−=(μ^+)†.
(24)

An optical operator acting through a cavity port would be a different choice and would require corresponding input–output and detection conventions. We follow the molecular-dipole response model of the paper.

For N=2, let B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩) and B2 be the basis from Section 11. The raising blocks are

[μ^+]1←0=μ0(011),[μ^+]2←1=μ0(000100100011).
(25)

The first column of the second matrix says that raising the molecular dipole on a one-photon ket produces |c,1⟩+|c,2⟩. Its second and third columns say that an already excited molecule cannot be raised again, but the other molecule can.

In a basis grouped by excitation number, the full dipole has a block-tridiagonal form:

[μ^]=(0[μ^−]0←10[μ^+]1←00[μ^−]1←20[μ^+]2←10).
(26)

At resonance, the ground-to-polariton dipoles have magnitude μ0N/2. The ideal dark kets have zero direct transition dipole from |0⟩. That optical darkness does not prohibit bath-mediated population transfer into them.

Section 14Deriving third-order response from the interaction Hamiltonian

Let the applied classical electric field be E(t), with interaction H^int(t)=−μ^E(t). In the interaction picture, the density operator obeys

dρ^I(t)dt=iℏE(t)[μ^I(t),ρ^I(t)].
(27)

Integrate this equation once, insert it into itself twice more, and collect the term cubic in the field. The chronological integrals impose ta<tb<tc<t:

ρ^I(3)(t)=(iℏ)3∫−∞tdtc∫−∞tcdtb∫−∞tbdtaE(tc)E(tb)E(ta)[μ^I(tc),[μ^I(tb),[μ^I(ta),ρ^eq]]].
(28)

The measured polarization is P(3)(t)=Tr(μ^I(t)ρ^I(3)(t)). For impulsive interactions separated by t1,t2,t3, introduce a forward propagation superoperator G^(t)A^=e−iH^t/ℏA^eiH^t/ℏ and a commutator superoperator μ^×A^=[μ^,A^]. Then

R(3)(t3,t2,t1)=(iℏ)3Tr[μ^G^(t3)μ^×G^(t2)μ^×G^(t1)μ^×ρ^eq].
(29)

The three intervals have different roles: t1 carries the first optical coherence, t2 is the waiting interval with populations or excited-state coherences, and t3 carries the emitted optical coherence. Absolute pulse times are 0,t1,t1+t2, with detection at t1+t2+t3. They must not be confused with the interval lengths.

For non-Markovian dynamics this compact expression acts on the full system–bath state, or on an equivalent extended representation that preserves the memory. Replacing each interval by a reduced map freshly initialized with a thermal bath is not generally equivalent.

Source: Eq. (8) and Eq. (15). Overall powers of ℏ are restored here; the propagation and detection phase conventions are specified below.

Section 15Liouville space: a commutator is an explicit matrix

Choose column-stacking vectorization. For a two-state basis (|0⟩,|e⟩), the Liouville basis is (|0⟩⟨0|,|e⟩⟨0|,|0⟩⟨e|,|e⟩⟨e|). The vectorized density operator is denoted |ρ⟩⟩. The identity

|A^X^B^⟩⟩=([B^]T⊗[A^])|X⟩⟩
(30)

gives left multiplication, right multiplication, and their difference as

[μ^L]=[I^]⊗[μ^],[μ^R]=[μ^]T⊗[I^],[μ^×]=[I^]⊗[μ^]−[μ^]T⊗[I^].
(31)

For [μ^]=μ0(0110),

[μ^×]=μ0(01−10100−1−10010−110).
(32)

Acting on |ρg⟩⟩=(1,0,0,0)T gives μ0(0,1,−1,0)T, corresponding to μ0(|e⟩⟨0|−|0⟩⟨e|). These opposite signs are the origin of the left- and right-side pathway signs.

For a Hamiltonian matrix, the propagation generator is

[L^H]=−iℏ([I^]⊗[H^]−[H^]T⊗[I^]),[G^(t)]=et[L^H].
(33)

The transpose is not a Hermitian conjugate. The formula follows from the chosen vectorization order; using a row-stacking implementation requires changing the Kronecker convention consistently.

Section 16Expand the nested commutator before drawing pathways

Write three successive optical operators as μ^1,μ^2,μ^3, suppressing propagation only for this algebraic expansion. The nested commutator contains eight terms:

[μ^3,[μ^2,[μ^1,ρ^]]]=μ^3μ^2μ^1ρ^−μ^3μ^2ρ^μ^1−μ^3μ^1ρ^μ^2+μ^3ρ^μ^1μ^2−μ^2μ^1ρ^μ^3+μ^2ρ^μ^1μ^3+μ^1ρ^μ^2μ^3−ρ^μ^1μ^2μ^3.
(34)

Each right multiplication contributes a minus sign. Reintroducing propagation between the interactions gives the Liouville pathways. The rotating-wave and phase-matching selections then retain particular raising/lowering choices, organized into the familiar six rephasing and nonrephasing pathways for the standard photon-echo experiment. The eight raw commutator terms and those six selected diagrams are different ways of organizing the calculation, not conflicting counts.

During a waiting interval, a pathway operator may be a population |a⟩⟨a|, an excited-state coherence |a⟩⟨b|, or a ground-state block. Individual pathway operators need not be positive density matrices; they are signed contributions to a perturbative response. A program must not renormalize them to unit trace after every pulse.

Section 17Six selected pathways, with signs and matrix actions

Define L^±A^=μ^±A^ and R^±A^=A^μ^±. In the table, the sequence is written chronologically from pulse one to pulse three; propagation occurs between entries. The sign shown is the product of the commutator signs, before the common response prefactor.

Signal Contribution First, second, third actions Sign
Rephasing Ground-state bleach (GSB) R^−,R^+,L^+ +
Rephasing Stimulated emission (SE) R^−,L^+,R^+ +
Rephasing Excited-state absorption (ESA) R^−,L^+,L^+ −
Nonrephasing GSB L^+,L^−,L^+ +
Nonrephasing SE L^+,R^−,R^+ +
Nonrephasing ESA L^+,R^−,L^+ −

For example, the first rephasing interaction acts on the right with a minus sign, giving a ground–excited coherence −|0⟩⟨a|. The second interaction can return it to +|0⟩⟨0| through right raising, or create −|b⟩⟨a| through left raising. The third interaction gives GSB from the ground branch, SE by right raising of the excited branch, and ESA by left raising into |f⟩⟨a|.

The same reasoning gives nonrephasing pathways starting with +|a⟩⟨0|. Detection uses Tr(μ^−A^) for the final raising coherence in this convention. Thus the spectrum combines GSB and SE with one sign and ESA with the opposite sign.

The article's discussion of absent SE cross-peaks in a particular nonrephasing polariton configuration should not be read as saying that nonrephasing SE pathways do not exist. Its Eq. (9) explicitly includes them. Whether a particular cross-peak survives depends on the state labels, dipole selection, and cancellations.

Source: Eq. (9), discussion of the nonrephasing cross-peaks, and Eq. (18). The left/right table is derived directly from the stated dipole convention.

Section 18A two-level pulse check and why ESA has a minus sign

Suppress propagation temporarily and set μ0=1. For one emitter, a first nonrephasing raising interaction gives A^1=|e⟩⟨0|. Acting with the lowering commutator gives

[μ^−,A^1]=|0⟩⟨0|−|e⟩⟨e|.
(35)

This is the trace-zero difference between a ground block and an excited block. A third raising commutator gives

[μ^+,|0⟩⟨0|−|e⟩⟨e|]=2|e⟩⟨0|.
(36)

One copy comes from GSB and one from SE. There is no doubly excited state for an isolated two-level emitter, so ESA is zero. For a multilevel or multi-emitter system, μ^+|e⟩ can be a two-excitation ket; its contribution comes from the negative excited block and has the ESA sign.

A useful complementary check is a harmonic ladder with linear dipole. Its transition amplitudes contain the bosonic square roots, and the third-order response of a purely quadratic Hamiltonian cancels. Failing this test often signals a missing ESA contribution, a wrong photon factor, a truncation too close to the populated levels, or an inconsistent Fourier phase.

Section 19From time-domain pathways to rephasing and absorptive spectra

For an optical coherence |a⟩⟨0|, forward evolution gives e−iωa0t; its conjugate |0⟩⟨a| gives e+iωa0t. This fixes the opposite excitation-axis transform signs:

R~r(ω1,t2,ω3)=∫0T1dt1∫0T3dt3ei(ω3t3−ω1t1)W1(t1)W3(t3)Rr(t3,t2,t1),
(37)
R~nr(ω1,t2,ω3)=∫0T1dt1∫0T3dt3ei(ω3t3+ω1t1)W1(t1)W3(t3)Rnr(t3,t2,t1).
(38)

The paper uses Wj(t)=cos⁡(πt/2Tj). Its displayed absorptive convention is

Sabs=−Im(R~r+R~nr).
(39)

Many implementations instead accumulate a pathway amplitude P without the common factor −i, so R=−iP. Then −ImR=ReP. Both forms agree only when that global phase is carried consistently. Taking the real part of a response that already includes the paper's −i prefactor would select the wrong quadrature.

The teaching code stores the signed pathway amplitudes without −i and uses their real part after Fourier transformation. It performs the two transform signs explicitly rather than relying on an unannotated FFT-axis flip.

Source: Eqs. (10)–(11). In particular, Eq. (11) uses minus the imaginary part; the alternative real-part convention is related by the displayed phase conversion.

Section 20Sampling, frequency resolution, and the rotating frame

If the sampled optical intervals have spacing Δt, the largest nonaliased angular frequency is π/Δt, or energy πℏ/Δt. A total sampled duration T gives a Fourier-grid spacing on the order of 2πℏ/T. Zero padding interpolates that grid but does not increase the physical information in the time record.

The electronic carrier near 2eV oscillates much faster than the polariton splittings. Subtracting a rotating-frame carrier ErefQ^, where Q^ counts total excitations, shifts an m-excitation block by mEref:

H^rot=H^s−ErefQ^.
(40)

All ground-to-first and first-to-second optical transitions are then shifted by the same reference energy. Subtracting ErefI^ from the entire Hamiltonian would only add a global phase and would not remove the optical carrier from density-matrix coherences.

Waiting-time coherences within the same excitation manifold are unchanged by this transformation. A reported upper–lower beat period must still be computed from the energy difference, not from the reference-subtracted energy of just one branch.

A numerical spectrum also requires a common phase reference for the rephasing and nonrephasing parts. Independent arbitrary phasing of each contribution can make a visually attractive plot while corrupting the nodal line and pathway cancellation.

Section 21Cavity loss as an operator, including the two-excitation manifold

Let κ be the photon-number decay rate in inverse time. A cavity linewidth parameter quoted as energy ΓE corresponds here to κ=ΓE/ℏ. The Markovian loss superoperator is

D^c(ρ^)=κ[a^ρ^a^†−12{a^†a^,ρ^}].
(41)

Through two excitations, the annihilator acts as

a^|c⟩=|0⟩,a^|2c⟩=2|c⟩,a^|c,n⟩=|n⟩,a^|n,m⟩=0.
(42)

For two emitters, concatenate the ground ket, the ordered one-excitation basis from Section 4, and the ordered two-excitation basis from Section 11. In that eight-state ordering, the only nonzero matrix entries are a0,c=1, ac,2c=2, a1,c1=1, and a2,c2=1. This sparse description specifies the entire eight-by-eight matrix.

The article explicitly displays the first-manifold loss operator |0⟩⟨c|. The annihilator above is its physical extension when the second manifold is retained. A derivation of ESA loss must include those additional actions rather than reusing only the one-excitation jump.

In column-stacked Liouville space,

[D^c]=κ([a^]∗⊗[a^]−12[I^]⊗[a^†a^]−12[a^†a^]T⊗[I^]).
(43)

The jump term transfers population into lower-excitation sectors. Keeping only the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian H^−iℏκa^†a^/2 describes conditional no-jump evolution, not the unconditional trace-preserving response. This distinction also matters for off-diagonal blocks: for example a^|2c⟩⟨c|a^†=2|c⟩⟨0|, a feed-down from an ESA optical coherence to a lower-manifold optical coherence.

Source: Eqs. (19)–(20). The full annihilator and explicit Liouville matrix are tutorial constructions for a consistent two-manifold calculation.

Section 22Deriving the polariton-to-dark relaxation estimate

A weak system–bath coupling estimate is useful for interpretation even when the production calculation is nonperturbative in the bath coupling. Define the two-sided unsymmetrized correlation transform

SB(ω)=∫−∞∞dteiωtC(t).
(44)

For a downward transition |α⟩→|β⟩, the golden-rule rate in the independent-bath model is

kα→β=1ℏ2∑n|⟨β|n^n|α⟩|2SB(Eα−Eβℏ).
(45)

The factor 1/ℏ2 follows from second order in an energy-valued coupling. With the energy-domain density defined in Section 10, positive frequencies obey SB(ω)=2ℏj(ℏω)[nB(ℏω)+1]. Using the dark-state sum from Section 9 gives

kU→D=N−1Nℏj(G)[nB(G)+1]at resonance,nB(G)=1eβG−1.
(46)

This rate samples the bath at G, not at 2G. For a Drude bath on its high-energy tail, j(G)∼2λγE/G; increasing the collective gap can therefore reduce this relaxation channel. A structured bath with a peak near G need not behave monotonically.

The rate estimate requires a weak-coupling and long-time approximation and neglects other pathways unless they are added explicitly. It is not a substitute for the full non-Markovian response calculation. The calculator labels it as a diagnostic proxy and does not fit the paper's reported lifetimes.

Section 23From population loss to coherence decay

For a Markovian secular model with jump L^βα=kα→β|β⟩⟨α|, the anticommutator contributes −kα→βραγ/2 to a coherence involving α≠γ. Summing losses from both endpoints gives

1T2=12∑β≠UkU→β+12∑β≠LkL→β+γφ.
(47)

Here γφ is additional relative pure dephasing within that approximation. At resonance, each polariton has photon fraction one half. The photon-loss contribution to 1/T2 is therefore κ/2. Keeping the upper-to-dark channel and neglecting other terms gives the paper's simple estimate

1T2≃kU→D2+κ2,T2≲2κ=2τcwithin this restricted rate model.
(48)

A full coupled Lindblad equation can mix polariton coherences and populations before a secular approximation, and a non-Markovian bath need not generate one exponential decay. The estimate explains a limiting scale; it is not an exact universal bound for every definition of a fitted cross-peak signal.

The disappearance of a spectroscopic cross-peak also does not necessarily equal the decay of a single reduced-density-matrix element. Dipole factors, competing pathways, bath memory in the optical intervals, and peak movement can all affect a chosen pixel or integrated region.

Source: Eqs. (12)–(14). The rate approximation and the full nonlinear simulation are kept separate here.

Section 24Beat periods, fitted envelopes, and what “200 fs” means

During the waiting interval, a coherence evolves approximately as

ρUL(t2)≃ρUL(0)e−i(EU−EL)t2/ℏe−t2/T2.
(49)

Interference with its conjugate gives a real oscillatory contribution. A useful fit is Acos⁡[(EU−EL)t2/ℏ+ϕ]e−t2/T2+B(t2), where B accounts for a nonoscillatory background. The angular inverse scale and full beat period differ by 2π:

τang=ℏEU−EL,Tbeat=2πℏEU−EL.
(50)

For a 140meV splitting, these are about 4.70fs and 29.54fs, respectively. For ΓE=10meV, the photon population lifetime is τc=ℏ/ΓE≃65.82fs.

The plotted envelope fits in the paper's Fig. 3 are labeled approximately 74, 100, and 122fs for collective couplings G≃35, 50, and 70meV. In an envelope e−t/T2, T2 is the amplitude's 1/e time. Its half-amplitude time is T2ln⁡2; 2T2 is not a separate mathematically defined coherence lifetime.

The abstract's statement of visible coherence extending to roughly 200fs should therefore be distinguished from the largest fitted exponential parameter, about 122fs. An oscillation can remain visible beyond one decay constant. This page keeps those two descriptions separate and uses the dimensionally explicit beat period above.

Quantity Definition Representative value
Bath correlation scale ℏ/γE about 295 fs
Photon population lifetime ℏ/ΓE about 65.8 fs
Full UP–LP beat period at 140 meV 2πℏ/(EU−EL) about 29.5 fs
Largest Fig. 3 fitted amplitude parameter parameter in e−t2/T2 about 122 fs

Source: Fig. 3, discussion of time scales, and Eq. (12). Values and terminology are separated so that an inverse angular frequency is not mislabeled as a full oscillation period.

Section 25Reading the reported two-dimensional spectra

The paper's Fig. 2 separates rephasing, nonrephasing, and total absorptive spectra for N=4. The two diagonal features follow the upper and lower polariton transitions. Cross-peaks connect their excitation and detection frequencies. The negative features arise from excited-state absorption and therefore depend on the two-excitation manifold.

Waiting-time oscillations occur because certain pathways carry |U⟩⟨L| or its conjugate during t2. Other pathways carry populations and contribute a background or slower redistribution. Calling every cross-peak an energy-transfer measurement would conflate coherence, population transfer, and interference between pathways.

Rephasing and nonrephasing signals have different line-shape elongations and different cancellations. The total absorptive map is not just a rescaled rephasing spectrum. In particular, the detailed ESA mismatch can leave residual nonrephasing cross-peaks even where an ideal harmonic picture would predict cancellation.

In the simulations used for the main comparison, the per-emitter coupling is approximately 24.8meV, so changing N=2,4,8 changes G as N. These results demonstrate the specified model trend; they should not be relabeled as a calculation at fixed collective splitting while varying N. A separate convergence study is needed for that distinct limit.

The paper explicitly treats bath memory and photon loss with L-PLDM. Its successful observation of prolonged simulated beating is therefore more informative than a two-state Hamiltonian oscillation without an environment, but it still inherits the physical model and approximate dynamical method used.

Section 26What is a nodal line, and how is its slope defined?

Near a lower-polariton diagonal peak, positive GSB/SE and negative ESA overlap. Their cancellation produces a zero contour of the absorptive signal. A chosen branch can be written as ω3=f(ω1;t2), satisfying Sabs(ω1,t2,f)=0. Differentiating implicitly gives

mNLS=∂f∂ω1=−∂Sabs/∂ω1∂Sabs/∂ω3on the selected zero contour.
(51)

This formula requires a nonzero denominator locally. Near a flat or noisy cancellation region, the slope becomes ill-conditioned. The angle θNLS=arctan⁡mNLS is meaningful only after specifying the units and scaling of both axes. A graph stretched horizontally changes the visual angle without changing the data-defined slope.

A nodal line is not the center line through maxima of a positive peak. It also is not an arbitrary zero of a dispersive quadrature. The correct signal phase and the inclusion of ESA are prerequisites for interpreting this particular diagnostic.

The paper finds flatter lower-polariton nodal lines at stronger collective coupling. This is interpreted as evidence of reduced vibrational dressing and altered spectral diffusion. The derivation of λα explains why that trend is plausible, but it does not establish a universal formula equating the nodal slope to λ/(4N).

Source: Figs. 4–5 and nodal-line discussion. The implicit-function derivation is a tutorial addition.

Section 27A solvable Gaussian model for a nodal line

Let x and y be excitation and detection energy offsets. Consider two equal-amplitude Gaussian lobes of opposite sign, with the same covariance and detection centers at y=±d/2:

S(x,y)=exp⁡[−Q(x,y−d/2)/2]−exp⁡[−Q(x,y+d/2)/2],
(52)
Q(x,y)=11−r2(x2σx2−2rxyσxσy+y2σy2),|r|<1.
(53)

At the node, the two exponentials are equal, so subtract their quadratic exponents. The x2 terms cancel. The remaining difference is proportional to −2dy/σy2+2rdx/(σxσy). Hence

y=rσyσxx,mNLS=rσyσx.
(54)

With equal axis widths the slope equals the correlation coefficient r, but this is a property of this specific two-Gaussian model. Unequal lobes, additional pathways, different widths, non-Gaussian bath dynamics, peak overlap, and a finite spectral window can change the relation.

Changing only the relative amplitudes while keeping the equal covariance in this simple model shifts the node's intercept; changing covariances can also change its slope. This distinction helps separate a line-shape correlation effect from a population-induced amplitude change.

The synthetic-node panel below verifies the formula by numerical root finding. It is not a reconstruction of a PNAS figure.

JavaScript is needed for the interactive calculation; the analytic slope is given immediately above.

Section 28Spectral diffusion from a fluctuating frequency

A simple illustrative frequency-noise model uses a zero-mean Gaussian fluctuation δω(t) with correlation Cω(t)=σω2e−|t|/τb. For an optical coherence, Gaussian averaging of its accumulated phase gives

⟨e−i∫0tδω(s)ds⟩=e−g(t),g(t)=∫0t(t−s)Cω(s)ds=σω2τb2(e−t/τb+t/τb−1).
(55)

At short times, g(t)≃σω2t2/2, producing Gaussian inhomogeneous broadening. At long times, g(t)≃σω2τbt apart from a constant, giving an exponential envelope. A static Gaussian component adds σstatic2t2/2 and does not decay away during a waiting interval.

A correlation between excitation and detection frequencies can therefore diminish as the environment loses memory over t2. But the amount of initial elongation and its decay time are different quantities. Collective dressing may reduce the fluctuation amplitude while leaving a slow environmental correlation time. A small slope at early waiting time is not necessarily evidence that every environmental mode has become fast.

For a quantum harmonic bath, the correlation also has an imaginary part related to response and reorganization. The real classical Gaussian model above illustrates line-shape geometry; it is not a replacement for the full quantum response or an exact formula for the paper's nodal-line dynamics.

Section 29Extracting a nodal line from numerical data

A reliable extraction begins with the correctly phased total absorptive spectrum. Choose a frequency region surrounding one lower-polariton feature and identify the same positive–negative boundary at each waiting time. For each excitation frequency, locate a sign-changing bracket along the detection axis and interpolate its root. Track the branch continuously rather than selecting whichever zero happens to be closest to the center at each step.

With samples (xi,yi) on the selected branch, fit yi=mxi+b over a stated interval. A weighted least-squares slope is

x¯w=∑iwixi∑iwi,y¯w=∑iwiyi∑iwi,m=∑iwi(xi−x¯w)(yi−y¯w)∑iwi(xi−x¯w)2.
(56)

Do not use roots in regions where both lobes are below a signal-to-noise threshold. Near ∂yS=0, a small signal error produces a large root error, δy≃−δS/(∂yS). This provides a natural warning flag and, with an uncertainty model, a weighting strategy.

Vary the fit window, time-domain apodization, Fourier duration, and sampling density. A physical slope trend should survive reasonable choices. The source's angles can be compared only using consistent axis units and a matching definition of the node.

For simulated trajectory data, bootstrap independent trajectory batches before extracting roots and fitting slopes. Bootstrapping the final root points alone can miss correlations caused by a shared trajectory ensemble.

Section 30What the L-PLDM calculation actually approximates

The source evaluates third-order correlation functions by a partially linearized density-matrix method, with stochastic treatment of Markovian photon loss. The basic distinction from a single mean-field trajectory is the simultaneous presence of forward and backward electronic mapping variables associated with the two sides of a density operator.

In a coordinate path integral, a density matrix has a forward nuclear path Q+(t) and a backward path Q−(t). Introduce mean and difference coordinates Q=(Q++Q−)/2, ΔQ=Q+−Q−. Expanding suitable nuclear action terms to first order in ΔQ is the partial-linearization step. Integration over the difference coordinate produces trajectory-like nuclear propagation while retaining separate quantum mapping amplitudes for the electronic branches. It is an approximation to the coupled quantum dynamics, not an exact replacement of every bath by classical noise.

For a harmonic bath initially thermal on the ground-state surface, the Wigner distribution is a product of Gaussians. In a mass-weighted mode,

⟨Qν2⟩W=ℏ2ωνcoth⁡βℏων2,⟨Pν2⟩W=ℏων2coth⁡βℏων2,⟨QνPν⟩W=0.
(57)

These widths include zero-point fluctuations. Replacing them by classical equipartition widths changes the initial bath sampling at low temperature or high frequency.

The paper's Eq. (17) writes a mapping estimator for propagation from a matrix element |a⟩⟨b|. Using its Gaussian mapping normalization, the segment estimator is

[ρ~(t)]ij∼[12ci(t)ca∗(0)][12c~j∗(t)c~b(0)],
(58)

followed by the prescribed mapping and bath averages. The factors one half belong to that sampling normalization. They must change if the mapping variables are rescaled or a different focused distribution is used. Here |c⟩=∑ici|i⟩ and |c~⟩=∑ic~i|i⟩ are the forward and backward mapping-amplitude kets; they are not independently normalized physical electronic wavefunctions by default.

Optical interactions connect these segment estimators through sums over electronic indices. The bath coordinates and their history continue through the pulse sequence. Resampling a fresh thermal bath at each pulse would destroy the inter-interval memory that the nonlinear response probes.

The estimator alone does not specify a working production algorithm: one also needs the mapping Hamiltonian, nuclear force convention, importance sampling, trajectory weights, and stochastic loss rules. Those details are supplied by the cited PLDM methods and the author's production repository. The finite-matrix teaching code accompanying this page does not pretend to implement L-PLDM.

Source: Eqs. (15)–(18), and the method references cited there. The mean/difference-coordinate discussion explains the approximation rather than asserting numerical exactness.

Section 31Why sparse propagation and Chebyshev expansion help

The number of basis kets grows quadratically with N through the second excitation manifold. A generic dense matrix–ket multiplication would cost the square of that dimension. But the HTC Hamiltonian only connects kets related by one photon–molecule exchange, so most entries are zero. Applying those connections directly avoids storing or multiplying a generic dense matrix.

For a time-independent Hermitian matrix over one short propagation step, shift and scale the Hamiltonian so that its spectrum lies in [−1,1]: H^′=(H^−bI^)/a, where a bounds the half-width and b is the spectral center. The propagator has the Chebyshev expansion

e−iH^Δt/ℏ=e−ibΔt/ℏ[J0(z)I^+2∑k=1∞(−i)kJk(z)Tk(H^′)],z=aΔtℏ.
(59)

The polynomial kets follow a three-term recurrence:

|v0⟩=|ψ⟩,|v1⟩=H^′|ψ⟩,|vk+1⟩=2H^′|vk⟩−|vk−1⟩.
(60)

Only repeated Hamiltonian actions are needed. The Bessel coefficients decay beyond the required polynomial order, providing a truncation criterion. Incorrect spectral bounds can destabilize the recurrence because the polynomials grow rapidly outside their intended interval.

Along a nuclear trajectory, the electronic Hamiltonian changes with time. Freezing it over a step or using a midpoint value introduces a separate time-discretization approximation even when the polynomial series for that frozen matrix is converged. Cavity-jump handling supplies another layer. These error controls should be tested independently of trajectory sampling convergence.

The source combines sparse Hamiltonian actions, Chebyshev propagation, and importance sampling of optical index sums. This is why it can explore the nonlinear response more efficiently than a naive dense implementation; it does not remove the need for convergence checks.

Source: Computational Approaches and the two JCP method papers cited there. The recurrence is shown explicitly to connect the numerical strategy to matrix–ket operations.

Section 32Explore polariton and bath scales

This panel uses the homogeneous Hamiltonian and the independently normalized bath convention in these notes. The relaxation output is a weak-coupling diagnostic at resonance, not a fitted reproduction of Fig. 3. Off resonance it reports the exact two-by-two mixing but does not apply the resonant dark-rate shortcut.

Interactive calculations require JavaScript. The static equations and worked examples remain readable without it.

A larger splitting does not automatically mean a narrower experimental line or a longer measured coherence. Detuning changes the matter/photon composition; correlated noise changes the averaging; structured baths change the resonant relaxation rate; and cavity linewidth changes the leakage scale. The panel isolates these analytic ingredients rather than combining them into an unsupported universal prediction.

Section 33Validation checks and source map

The companion pnas_teaching_model.py generates the excitation-truncated basis, Hamiltonian, local projector matrices, dipole blocks, and photon annihilator. It can calculate a small-system rephasing and nonrephasing spectrum with cavity loss. Its purpose is to make the operator algebra and phase conventions inspectable. It omits the molecular non-Markovian bath and is not the PNAS figure-generation code.

Useful tests are independent of whether a spectrum looks plausible. Check Hermiticity of the Hamiltonian, [H^s,Q^]=0, the analytic one- and two-excitation eigenvalues, dipole selection rules, trace preservation of the Lindblad generator, and conservation of the excitation difference between ket and bra under cavity jump feed-down. Compare explicit commutators with their Kronecker representations and verify that ESA disappears for an isolated two-level system.

For a research reproduction, also converge the bath discretization, trajectory count, propagation step, optical time windows, waiting-time resolution, excitation truncation, and nodal-line extraction. Compare the plotted observable directly: a reduced-density-matrix coherence, a single-pixel signal, a region-integrated peak, and a fitted oscillatory residual are not identical quantities.

Section 34Worked exercises

1. Verify the two-molecule bright transformation.

In (|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩), use columns (1,0,0)T, (0,1,1)T/2, and (0,1,−1)T/2. Multiplication gives a cavity–bright coupling 2gE and zero cavity–dark coupling. Both molecular diagonal entries remain ϵ.

2. Obtain the resonant reorganization energy for eight emitters.

Each molecular probability in one polariton is 1/(2N)=1/16. Squaring and summing over eight sites gives 8/256=1/32. Thus λα=50/32=1.5625cm−1. This is a diagonal-dressing scale, not a fitted dephasing rate.

3. Sum the dark-state channels.

For N=8, each normalized dark channel carries a summed squared projector matrix element 1/(2N)=1/16. Seven such destinations give 7/16. Increasing N does not make this total vanish; spectral filtering at the gap remains important.

4. Count the retained basis for two and eight emitters.

For N=2, the dimensions are 1,3,4, totaling eight. For N=8, they are 1,9,37, totaling 47. A dense Liouville representation therefore has 64 or 2209 components, respectively, even before introducing an explicit bath or auxiliary memory representation.

5. Check the two-photon factor.

The exchange gEσ^n†a^ acting on |2c⟩ gives 2gE|c,n⟩. The same exchange acting on |c,m⟩ with n≠m gives gE|n,m⟩. For n=m, it vanishes because (σ^n†)2=0.

6. Show that a cavity jump can transfer an ESA coherence.

Use a^|2c⟩=2|c⟩ and ⟨c|a^†=⟨0|. Then a^|2c⟩⟨c|a^†=2|c⟩⟨0|. The excitation difference remains one, but both sides have lost one photon.

7. Convert a 140 meV splitting to a full beat period.

Use T=2πℏ/ΔE, giving 2π(658.2119569)/140≃29.54fs. The number 658.2119569/140≃4.70fs is the inverse angular frequency and lacks the 2π needed for a full period.

8. Convert an exponential parameter to a half-amplitude time.

Set e−t/T2=1/2. Taking logarithms gives t=T2ln⁡2. For T2=122fs, this is about 84.6fs. At t=2T2, the amplitude is e−2≃0.135 of its initial value, not zero.

9. Find a synthetic nodal-line angle.

For r=0.3,σx=12meV,σy=10meV, the slope is m=0.3(10/12)=0.25. With identical energy units on both axes, arctan⁡(0.25)≃14.04∘. A different plotting aspect ratio would change the visual angle but not this data-defined result.

10. Check the real-part versus imaginary-part convention.

Let P=a+ib and R=−iP=b−ia. Then −ImR=a=ReP. The two absorptive formulas agree only after this phase conversion. Applying Re directly to R instead would return b, the other quadrature.

11. Verify trace preservation of the dissipator.

Cyclicity gives Tr(a^ρ^a^†)=Tr(a^†a^ρ^). Each anticommutator term has the same trace, and the two half factors cancel the jump trace. Thus Tr[D^c(ρ^)]=0, including for non-Hermitian pathway operators.

12. Why must the rotating-frame shift use excitation number?

A transition between manifolds m and m+1 changes its energy by −Eref under H^−ErefQ^. Subtracting ErefI^ shifts both levels equally and leaves every transition unchanged. The former removes the carrier; the latter is only an overall energy-origin change.
